questions.q: A file's first line logs "starting". Line 20 has a missing bracket. What happens when you run the file?
questions.explain: A syntax error is an early error: parsing fails, so there is no program to run. A runtime error, by contrast, happens at one line after the earlier lines have run.
options: "starting" is printed, then the program crashes at line 20
Nothing is printed: the engine parses the whole file first and reports a SyntaxError before running any of it
The engine skips line 20 and runs the rest
It depends on whether line 20 is ever reached

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new Function parses the source immediately. The missing ) fails the parse, so the function is never created: neither "prepared" nor "reserving stock" prints.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The code is valid syntax, so it parses. It fails at run time on order.total, after the first line has already run.

questions.q: In which order does an engine like V8 process your code?
questions.explain: The scanner produces tokens, the parser builds an AST, the bytecode generator produces bytecode for the interpreter, and hot functions are compiled to optimized machine code while the program runs.
options: Bytecode, tokens, syntax tree, machine code
Tokens, syntax tree, bytecode (interpreted), optimized machine code for hot functions
Machine code first, then bytecode if it fails

questions.q: What does the scanner (lexer) produce from total = price * qty; // line total?
questions.explain: Scanning groups characters into the words of the language and throws away whitespace and comments. Building structure from the tokens is the parser's job.
options: A syntax tree with an assignment node
Tokens: total, =, price, *, qty, ; (the comment and spaces are dropped)

questions.q: In the syntax tree for price - 500 * qty, where is the multiplication?
questions.explain: Higher-precedence operations sit deeper in the tree and are evaluated first. The subtraction's right operand is the whole product 500 * qty.
options: At the root, with the subtraction as its left child
As the right child of the subtraction, so it is computed first
Next to the subtraction, at the same level
There is no multiplication node; it is folded into a constant

questions.q: Why does V8 start by interpreting bytecode instead of compiling everything to optimized machine code immediately?
questions.explain: Optimizing everything up front would make startup slow, and the optimizer would not yet know what types the code really sees. So the engine interprets first and optimizes the hot functions.
options: Most code runs only a few times; starting quickly matters more, and the interpreter collects type feedback that makes later optimization better
Bytecode is always faster than machine code

questions.q: What does "just-in-time" compilation mean?
questions.explain: A JIT compiler works during execution, using the type feedback the interpreter gathered. Ahead-of-time compilers work before the program runs.
options: Compiling the program before it is shipped
Compiling functions to machine code while the program runs, based on how they have been used so far
Compiling only when a syntax error occurs

questions.q: A hot function optimized for integers is suddenly called with a string. What happens?
questions.explain: Deoptimization only affects speed, never results. The optimized code's assumption no longer holds, so the engine falls back to bytecode and may re-optimize later with wider assumptions.
options: A guard fails, the engine deoptimizes (drops the machine code) and continues in the interpreter with the correct result
The string is converted to an integer permanently

questions.q: Which habit helps hot code stay optimized, and is also simply correct?
questions.explain: Parse a form's "950000" into a number when it arrives. Inner functions then see one type, which the JIT likes, and you avoid bugs such as "950000" + 2 giving "9500002".
options: Converting input to the right type once, at the edge, so inner functions always see the same types
Adding properties to objects as late as possible

questions.q: What is a hidden class (V8's "map")?
questions.explain: Objects created the same way share a hidden class, so the engine can read a property with one memory access, remembered by an inline cache.
options: A class declared with the #private syntax
The engine's internal description of an object's layout: which properties it has, in which order, and where each is stored
A class that is not exported from a module

questions.q: This runs in Node.js with V8's internal %HaveSameMap enabled. What does it print?
questions.explain: a and b have the same properties in the same order, so they share a hidden class. c has them in the other order, which is a different hidden class.

questions.q: Which way of creating order objects keeps one hidden class for all of them?
questions.explain: Same properties, same order, set in one place, means one shape. Adding or deleting properties later creates new shapes.
options: Add coupon only to the orders that have one
Build each order with properties in whatever order the data arrives
Create every order in one factory or constructor with all properties, using null for "no coupon"
Delete unused properties after creating the object

questions.q: A file contains 500 functions, and only 10 are called at startup. What does lazy parsing do with the other 490?
questions.explain: Pre-parsing is cheaper than a full parse but still checks the syntax, which is why an error anywhere stops the file.
options: Ignores them completely, so their syntax errors are never found
Pre-parses them quickly (finding syntax errors and the variables they use) and fully parses each one only when it is first called
Compiles all of them to machine code at startup

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In the creation phase, function declarations get their function and var gets undefined. The assignment discount = 0.1 only happens in the execution phase, later.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: vatRate exists from the creation phase, but a const is uninitialised until its line runs. Reading it before then throws a ReferenceError (the temporal dead zone).

questions.q: A function creates an order object and returns it. When the function returns, what happens?
questions.explain: Frames live on the stack and disappear on return. Objects live on the heap; the returned reference keeps the order alive.
options: The object is freed with the function's stack frame
The stack frame is removed; the object stays on the heap as long as something refers to it
The object is copied onto the caller's stack

questions.q: Which of these is provided by the host (browser or Node.js), not by the JavaScript engine itself?
questions.explain: The language defines Promise, Map and JSON. Timers, I/O and the event loop come from the host that embeds the engine.

questions.q: Who decides which callback runs next when the call stack is empty?
questions.explain: The engine runs a function until the stack is empty, then its microtasks. Which task comes next (a timer, a request, a click) is the host's decision.
options: The host's event loop, which hands the engine the next task (then the engine drains the microtasks)

questions.q: An error is thrown inside a setTimeout callback. Why does its stack trace not show the function that called setTimeout?
questions.explain: Each task starts with an empty stack. To keep the scheduling context, log ids in the callback, or create an Error at scheduling time and attach it as a cause.
options: The callback runs later as a new task with an empty stack; the scheduling function returned long ago
Stack traces only work in synchronous code

questions.q: This prints the names of your own functions found in an error's stack trace. What does it print?
questions.explain: After await, V8 knows which async function is waiting on the current one and adds it to the trace, marked async: zero-cost async stack traces.

questions.q: Compared with an await chain, why does an error thrown inside a .then callback after a timer often have a short, unhelpful stack trace?
questions.explain: Async stack traces come from awaiting async functions. A plain callback chain gives the engine nothing to reconstruct the story from.
options: The callback runs from the microtask queue after a timer task, with nothing of yours below it on the stack, and no async functions are awaiting it to add frames
It has the same trace as await

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The stack is recorded when the Error object is created, inside makeError, not where it is thrown. So the top frame is makeError, then reserve.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Error.captureStackTrace(error, invalid) records the stack starting below invalid, so the first frame is setPrice, where the bad value came in.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: V8 records at most Error.stackTraceLimit frames (10 by default in V8, so in Node.js and Chrome). With 31 nested calls and a limit of 10, only 10 appear; lowering the limit to 5 records 5. The setting is global, so the code restores it.

questions.q: A production stack trace points at dist/app.js:1:48213, a minified bundle. What connects it back to your TypeScript source?
questions.explain: A source map records how positions in generated code correspond to positions in the original files, so traces can show your own file names and lines.
options: A source map, used by Node.js with --enable-source-maps and by browser developer tools

questions.q: Why must the pricing-rule engine not run staff formulas with new Function("return " + rule)?
questions.explain: Parsing into a tree you control, with a whitelist of names and operators, guarantees only arithmetic can run. Generating code from that tree is then safe.
options: It is code injection: any JavaScript in the text would run with the server's full power
The result would be a string

questions.q: Where does the rule engine check that a formula only uses allowed names?
questions.explain: Checking as early as possible means the later stages can trust their input. It also reports the problem with a position when the rule is saved.
options: In the compiled function, at checkout
In the tokenizer, the very first stage, so a disallowed name never reaches the parser or the evaluator

questions.q: How does the recursive descent parser make * bind more tightly than +?
questions.explain: Each precedence level is its own grammar rule, and lower levels call higher ones. Precedence falls out of the structure, with no special cases.
options: It sorts the operators before parsing
The rule for +/- (expression) calls the rule for *// (term) for its operands, so products are built first, deeper in the tree
It uses a lookup table at run time

questions.q: Why is the compiled rule faster than the tree-walking interpreter when run over 300,000 cart lines?
questions.explain: An interpreter repeats the same decisions on every evaluation. Compiling does them once, which is the same trade a JIT makes for hot functions.
options: The compiled rule skips the arithmetic
The decisions about the tree (which node, which operator) are made once, and the engine can optimize the generated function like any hot code
new Function runs on another thread

questions.q: What does this tiny interpreter print?
questions.explain: The tree is (price - 500) * qty: the subtraction is a child of the multiplication, so it is evaluated first: (2500 - 500) * 3 = 6000.

questions.q: Finish tokenize(source) for rules made of whole numbers, the names price and qty, and the characters + - * / ( ). Skip spaces. Throw a SyntaxError with the message unexpected "X" at position N for anything else.
questions.explain: A scanner reads characters in a loop and groups runs of digits or letters into single tokens. Anything that is not part of the language is rejected with its position.
questions.expected:
( | price | - | 500 | ) | * | qty
SyntaxError: unexpected "%" at position 6

questions.q: Finish evaluate(node, vars) for trees with number, name and binary nodes (operators + - * /).
questions.explain: A tree-walking interpreter is a recursive function with one case per node type. Binary nodes evaluate both children first, then apply their operator.

questions.q: Finish emit(node) so it turns a tree into JavaScript source: numbers as themselves, names as vars.NAME, binary nodes as (LEFT OP RIGHT). The compiled function is built from it.
questions.explain: Wrapping every binary node in parentheses preserves the tree's structure in the generated code, so precedence cannot change. The code is generated from the checked tree, never from raw user text.

questions.q: Finish validationError(message) so the returned error's stack trace starts at the caller: use Error.captureStackTrace to leave the helper out.
questions.explain: Error.captureStackTrace(target, fn) re-records the stack, omitting fn and everything above it, so the trace begins where the bad value came in.
questions.expected: quantity must be at least 1 | top frame is setQuantity: true

questions.q: A callback scheduled with setTimeout fails, and its stack trace cannot show who scheduled it. Create an Error("scheduled here") at scheduling time and attach it as the cause of the error you log from the callback.
questions.explain: An Error captures the stack when it is created. Creating one while scheduleSms is still on the stack preserves the scheduling context that the timer task would otherwise lose.
questions.expected: SMS for order 9 failed | cause stack mentions scheduleSms: true

questions.q: Orders are built in two places with different property orders, and some get coupon added later. Write one factory makeOrder(id, totalKobo, coupon) that always creates { id, totalKobo, coupon } in that order, with coupon defaulting to null, and use it for both orders.
questions.explain: One factory means one set of properties in one order, so all orders share a hidden class, and null marks "no coupon" without changing the shape.
